li.a: Amnesty International: Sri Lanka, the "disappearances" from Eastern University Refugee Camp on 5 September 1990 (October 1993)
Amnesty International: Sri Lanka, When will justice be done? (1994)
Tamil Guardian: 30th anniversary of Eastern University disappearances and massacre commemorated
Tamil Guardian: Eastern University disappearances and massacre remembered 32 years on
Tamil Guardian: Eastern University commemorates 34th anniversary of disappearances by Sri Lankan army
Tamil Guardian: 158 Tamils disappeared from Eastern Uni in 1990 round-up remembered in Batticaloa

content.p: On the morning of 5 September 1990, soldiers entered a refugee camp that had grown up on the campus of Eastern University at Vantharumoolai, near Batticaloa in eastern Sri Lanka. They sorted the men and boys into lines, and 158 people were taken away on buses after masked informers pointed them out. The soldiers said the men would be released after questioning. By the account of the Human Rights Task Force, a body the Sri Lankan government itself set up, not one of them was traced afterwards. Amnesty International, which counted 159, called it a case in which people were taken in front of thousands of witnesses, some willing to testify, without any official inquiry being held.

No bodies have ever been found. The Tamil Guardian reports that locals believe those taken were probably massacred, and the event is described both as a disappearance and as a massacre. Responsibility rests on the testimony of witnesses and on an official task force's findings rather than on any court verdict. No prosecution has been reported.
content.h2: Fleeing the fighting in the east
content.p: The Tamil Guardian places the event in the aftermath of the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) gaining a stronghold in the Eastern Province in 1990. The army answered with a military operation that pushed towards Batticaloa and quickly set up bases in the surrounding district. Amnesty International's 1994 report likewise describes people who had taken refuge at the camp as having fled their homes amid fighting between government troops and the LTTE.

Civilians sought safety in public places, among them places of worship and schools. According to the Tamil Guardian, refugees in such places were rounded up by the military, intense searches followed, and many of those taken away for questioning never came back. The campus at Vantharumoolai was one of these shelters. The Human Rights Task Force account, which Amnesty reproduced, says nearly 45,000 refugees were in the camp. Amnesty's own 1994 report says "thousands".

The Task Force account was based on interviews carried out by its chairman and its regional manager in Batticaloa. It says a group of soldiers, many from the 8 Brigade headquarters at Valaichenai, reached the camp early in the morning in several jeeps, bringing two buses with them. Women were told to stand to one side. Men were told to form three lines.

Two hooded men stood with the soldiers, and the lines were made to walk past them. Each time a hooded man nodded, the man or boy in front of him was taken into custody. The Task Force wrote that the people picked out included the young and the old, and that at least one was only 11 years old. In all, 158 people were chosen this way. Their hands were tied behind their backs and they were put into the two buses while parents and relatives watched. Amnesty's 1994 report, using a count of 159, says witnesses saw about 50 uniformed soldiers take the detainees away in five vehicles, and that most of those taken were young men between 16 and 40. The two figures for vehicles and for people are in conflict and are given here as each source gave them.

A separate incident took place inside the campus that day. The Task Force account says a group of LTTE men who had taken refuge at the university ignored the army's order to line up outside and hid in the assembly hall. A bomb blast went off inside the hall, "accidentally or otherwise" in the Task Force's words, killing some of those in hiding and badly injuring others, who were taken away in the jeeps. The Task Force said the blast "no doubt added to the acrimony of the proceedings".

The university authorities, the account adds, had kept a list of the people taken, because they were responsible for the refugees sheltering on the campus. Amnesty published that list of 159 names with ages and occupations where known. It includes students, labourers, businessmen, farmers, fishermen, a teacher, a cashier, a railway guard and a goldsmith, and men aged from their mid-teens to their seventies.

The Task Force found that official answers to the relatives and to local representatives contradicted each other. On 17 October 1990, the secretary to the defence minister, Air Marshal A. W. Fernando, replied to inquiries that only 32 people had been taken from the Vantharumoolai camp on 5 September. He listed 31 names and said they had been taken only for questioning and had been released within 24 hours. The Task Force wrote that none of the people said to have been released reached home. It pointed out that the list included an 11-year-old and a 16-year-old, and that one of the names, N. Stanley, 35, belonged to a man from Vantharumoolai whose wife was later told otherwise.

That happened in July 1993, at the Presidential Mobile Services in Batticaloa. Stanley's wife complained of her husband's disappearance and received a reply, on a standard duplicated form, saying he had never been taken by the authorities. The Task Force called this "the supreme gaffe", since the defence ministry had named him among those taken and released.

A second answer came after the Government Agent apparently wrote to the army on 22 September 1990 about the incident, in the Task Force's wording. Major S. Seneviratne of 8 Brigade headquarters replied on 29 October 1990 that his troops had searched the camp and questioned more than 200 of its inmates, and that no one had been held. A third version had already gone out on the evening news bulletin of the state broadcaster, the Sri Lanka Broadcasting Corporation, on 7 September 1990, which announced that the army had taken 148 people into custody from the camp for inquiries.

Amnesty added, in a passage on the round-ups that followed, that a local member of parliament raised the Eastern University disappearances in Parliament in September 1990, and that to its knowledge no independent investigation had been carried out.

The Task Force published its account in its second annual report, dated 29 September 1993 and covering August 1992 to August 1993. The government had established the Task Force in August 1991 to monitor the welfare of detainees. Its report named four officers whom witnesses said were involved, and said they were from the Chenkalady army camp, the Valaichenai camp, the Batticaloa camp and the National Intelligence Bureau in Batticaloa. One of the four was said to use an assumed name, and the Task Force wrote that most witnesses could identify one captain, who it said was widely feared and well known among the public at the time. The names were not given in the version Amnesty reproduced, and are not repeated here, because no court has tested the allegations.

The Task Force asked for a proper investigation, for compensation for the bereaved families, many of whom had lost their breadwinners, and for death certificates. Amnesty asked the government what it had done to investigate the allegations since the report. In 1994, Amnesty wrote that in spite of the Task Force's work and the naming of four officers, the government had taken no action to investigate. It urged a full, impartial and independent investigation, the bringing to justice of those found responsible, and compensation for relatives.

The Eastern University round-up was one of several in the district that month. Amnesty's 1994 report records that on 9 September 1990 soldiers took into custody villagers from four places in the district (38 from Saturukondan, 80 from Kokkuvil and smaller numbers from two other villages), and that 68 of those reported disappeared were children. The Tamil Guardian says soldiers and Muslim home guards rounded up 186 Tamils from Sathurukondan and surrounding villages and killed them, a figure and a description of events that differ from Amnesty's. It adds that a further 16 people were arrested two weeks after the Eastern University round-up and disappeared, and that their fates are unknown.

Thangamuthu Jayasingam, who was the officer in charge of the Vantharumoolai camp at the time, wrote in 2015 that he had spoken to national and international figures, and that he had testified before the Presidential Commission on Missing Persons in 2004. He said he gave the commission the names of the army officers who had come that day, together with the name of an army major general who visited the camp three days later, on 8 September. He wrote that he did not know whether any inquiry had been held since.

On the 34th anniversary the Tamil Guardian reported that a Presidential Commission report had confirmed that, according to witnesses, the army had detained 158 people that day, and that nothing further had come of it. The Jaffna Monitor, in an analysis of Sri Lanka's disappearances published in August 2026, says the Task Force named four officers on the strength of witness interviews, but that no one was ever prosecuted. It calls the case one of the largest single mass-disappearance events of the conflict.

The wider record bears out that gap. The Jaffna Monitor reports that the commissions which investigated disappearances province by province between 1994 and 2001 attributed about 90 percent of the enforced disappearances in the north-east to the Sri Lankan military and police, and about 10 percent to paramilitary groups including the LTTE. It also notes that fewer than 500 indictments have followed more than 20,000 documented cases.

Relatives of the disappeared have marked the anniversary in several years. The Tamil Guardian reported that on the 27th anniversary families gathered at a temple in Arumugathankudiyirippu, Batticaloa, at an event organised by Eastern University students. On the 30th anniversary a vigil was held in front of the Vantharumoolai campus, organised by the Batticaloa families of the disappeared, with relatives holding placards and photographs. The 32nd anniversary was marked again, and on the 34th the Batticaloa Association of Relatives of the Enforced Disappeared and the university's Faculty of Arts and Culture Students' Union held a gathering at the campus, observing a minute of silence and lighting candles.
The Tamil Guardian reported on the 30th anniversary that relatives remained hopeful their loved ones were alive and were urging justice and inquiries into their whereabouts.
